title: Looped Diffusion Transformer: the same blocks run several times inside each denoising step, and loop depth can be changed at sampling time [R]
summary: Paper: Looped Diffusion Transformer (arXiv 2609.40305, 30 Sep). Instead of making a text-to-image DiT bigger, it runs a shared group of transformer blocks several times inside each denoising step. The authors report that naive looping doesn't reliably help, and fix it with deep supervision on every loop plus self-modulating attention. Their headline claims: a 260M looped model beats a model 6.5x larger on several benchmarks with 4.9x less inference compute, and at a fixed inference budget, more loop depth helps more than more denoising steps.The B/16 code and weights are MIT (the weights are on Hugging Face under sensenova), so I ran it on an M5 Pro: PyTorch MPS in fp32, 100 Euler steps, CFG 6.0, and one seed per prompt reused at loop depths 1 to 4. It was trained at depth 4, and the README says other depths work without retraining. The grid shows five of the prompts I tried.Most of the change happens before depth 3, and depths 3 and 4 come out very close on every prompt shown. The interesting part to me is that depth is picked at sampling time, the way the iteration count is in looped and recurrent-depth language models, so you can trade compute for refinement per image. On this machine an image took about 23 to 24 seconds at depth 1 and 43 to 47 at depth 4.submitted by/u/Fit-Ant2238[link][comments]
title_es: Looped Diffusion Transformer: eficiencia mediante bloques reutilizables
bajada: Nuevo paper presenta Looped Diffusion Transformer, que reutiliza bloques de transformers dentro de cada paso de denoising, logrando resultados comparables con modelos 6.5x más grandes usando 80% menos compute. La aproximación permite ajustar profundidad en tiempo de inferencia.
bajada_en: New paper presents Looped Diffusion Transformer, which reuses transformer blocks within denoising steps, matching results of 6.5x larger models with 80% less compute. The approach allows depth adjustment at inference time.

title: SWE-Duel: Towards a Self-Scaling Arena for Coding Agents
summary:
arXiv:2610.12569v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Static coding benchmarks are fixed at release. Over time their tasks leak into training data, and stronger agents eventually saturate them. We argue that a benchmark should instead aim to be self-scaling: its tasks and oracles are created at evaluation time, so no content exists in advance to leak, and its difficulty is set by the participating agents rather than fixed at release. We introduce SWE-Duel, an arena in which two coding agents evaluate each other over mirrored Red-Blue turns. In each turn, the Red agent works on a real repository across three context-isolated sessions. It proposes and implements a new feature with feature tests, then embeds a subtle bug in that feature along with sealed bug-triggering tests. The resulting pull request is admitted only if (1) it passes the feature tests and the repository's existing tests while failing exactly the bug tests, and (2) a fresh session of the same agent can repair the bug blind, which rules out unsolvable tasks. The Blue agent then reviews the pull request without being told a bug exists. It wins only if its revision passes all three test suites, and then the two agents swap roles. We run a tournament among 11 model-harness participants on 15 repositories in five languages for 1,500 turns. The leaders win in different ways. GPT-5.5 with Codex CLI ranks first as the strongest solver, repairing 98.3% of the defects it reviews. Claude Opus 4.8 with mini-swe-agent ranks second as the strongest task author, with a 27.3% Red win rate. Finally, within one model family, tasks written by the newest version defeat a fixed-reference solver far more often than those of older versions (42.9% vs. 4.0%), giving preliminary evidence that task difficulty scales with task authoring capability.
title_es: SWE-Duel: arena auto-escalable para evaluar agentes de codificación
bajada: Researchers proponen SWE-Duel, un benchmark que se auto-escala en tiempo de evaluación para evitar saturación y filtración de tareas en datos de entrenamiento. Los agentes se evalúan mutuamente proponiendo features y bugs, creando desafíos dinámicos.
bajada_en: Researchers propose SWE-Duel, a benchmark that self-scales at evaluation time to prevent saturation and task leakage into training data. Agents evaluate each other by proposing features and bugs, creating dynamic challenges.

summary: Neoclouds and so-called inference providers that help app developers run open source models are trying to differentiate themselves in a very crowded market.For instance, one such neocloud,Prime Intellect, which was valued at $1 billion in an equity financing in July, is buying a startup to help it make open models run faster and more cheaply on itsNvidiaservers, compared to its rivals.Prime Intellect, based in San Francisco, is acquiringMoondream, a young developer of open-source models that has fewer than 10 employees, according to Prime Intellect co-founder and CEOVincent Weisser.
